EXPLANATION

Newton’s second law states that F=ma, where F is the resultant force, m is the mass, and a is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we first differentiate r to get the velocity vector:

v=drdt=⟨ddt(t3),ddt(t4−t2)⟩=⟨3t2,4t3−2t⟩

Next, we differentiate the velocity vector to get the acceleration vector:

a=dvdt=⟨ddt(3t2),ddt(4t3−2t)⟩=⟨6t,12t2−2⟩

Therefore, the resultant force F at time t equals

F=ma=3⋅⟨6t,12t2−2⟩=⟨18t,36t2−6⟩.

When t=4s, we have

F(4)=⟨18(4),36(42)−6⟩=⟨72,570⟩.

Finally, the magnitude of F(4) is given by

|F(4)|=(72)2+(570)2≈575N

rounded to the nearest Newton.
name: Question 15
problem:
The displacement $r,$ in meters, of a particle $P$ of mass $3\,\text{kg}$ is given by

$$
r=⟨{t}^{3},\,{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}⟩,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force acting on the particle when $t=4\,\text{s}.$ Round your final answer to the nearest Newton.
worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we first differentiate $r$ to get the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}-{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},\,4{t}^{3}-2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate the velocity vector to get the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{3}-2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨6t,\,12{t}^{2}-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =3\cdot ⟨6t,\,12{t}^{2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨18t,\,36{t}^{2}-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=4\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(4) & =⟨18(4),\,36({4}^{2})-6⟩ \\  & =⟨72,\,570⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of $F(4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|F(4)| & =\sqrt{(72)^{2}+{(570)}^{2}} \\  & ≈575\,\text{N}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest Newton.
